sections.heading: What Is a JPG Compressor?
sections.body:
A JPG compressor is an image optimization tool that reduces the amount of data used to store a photograph. JPG uses lossy compression. This means some image information is discarded during encoding to create a smaller file. The amount of information removed depends on the compression settings.

A stronger compression setting can create a smaller file, but it can also affect visible details. Fine textures, faces, lettering and sharp edges may show changes when the quality is reduced too much. FileCompresser provides different quality options so you can choose a result according to the purpose of your photograph.

sections.heading: How to Compress a JPG Image Online
sections.body:
1. Select a JPG, JPEG or JFIF image and wait for validation.
2. Open Settings and choose Balanced, High Quality, Maximum or Target Size.
3. Choose Compress.
4. Compare the original and output at the same scale.
5. Download a suitable result and keep your source.

Multiple supported images can share a queue. Settings apply to the selected files, and each result can be reviewed separately.

sections.heading: Understanding JPG Compression Settings
sections.body: The right setting depends on how you intend to use your image.

sections.heading: Maximum Compression
sections.body: Maximum is useful when reducing file size is the main priority. It applies a stronger quality trade-off and may produce more visible changes than other settings. This option can be useful for photographs that need to meet strict upload requirements, provided the final image remains clear enough.

sections.heading: Balanced Compression
sections.body: Balanced provides a more moderate quality and file size trade-off. It is a practical starting point when you need a smaller JPG without using the strongest available compression.

sections.heading: High Quality Compression
sections.body: High Quality is suitable when you want to retain more visual detail. The resulting file may be larger, but it can be a better choice for product photographs, portraits and images containing important details.

sections.heading: Target Size Compression
sections.body:
Sometimes an upload form requires a photograph below a specific file size. In this situation, a general quality preset may not be enough. The Target Size option searches for actual encodes and verifies the final file size in bytes. For example, a 50 KB maximum means 50,000 bytes.

It is important to understand that the requested size is a limit, not a promise that the final image will have exactly that number of bytes. If no suitable encoding meets the selected limit, the tool reports Target not met.

sections.heading: Can You Compress a JPG to 50KB?
sections.body: Target Size lets you set a maximum of 50 KB, meaning 50,000 bytes. A detailed photograph may not fit at its original dimensions within the available encoding settings. If the target cannot be reached, choose a larger limit or consider a supported format conversion. Preparing smaller dimensions in a separate image editor is another option; this site does not resize images. Always check whether faces, text and other required details remain readable.

sections.heading: Why Compress JPG Images?
sections.body: There are several practical reasons to reduce JPG file size.

sections.heading: Meet Online Upload Requirements
sections.body: Government forms, job applications, educational portals and other websites may restrict the size of uploaded photographs. A JPG compressor can help prepare an image for these requirements.

sections.heading: Reduce Email Attachment Size
sections.body: Large photographs can make email attachments difficult to send. A smaller JPG is easier to attach and share, especially when several pictures need to be included.

sections.heading: Optimize Website Photographs
sections.body: Website owners often use JPG images for product pages, blog posts and galleries. Reducing unnecessary image data can help lower the amount of information visitors need to download.

sections.heading: Save Storage Space
sections.body: Smaller photographs use less storage space when saved across folders, devices and backup systems. This can be helpful when managing large collections of images.

sections.heading: Does JPG Compression Reduce Image Quality?
sections.body:
Yes, lossy JPEG encoding can change image quality. The extent of the change depends on the selected settings and original photograph. A lower-quality setting can affect fine details, gradients, skin textures and small text. The changes may be difficult to notice in some photographs but more visible in detailed images.

Always compare the original and compressed versions at the same size. Do not judge an image only by its thumbnail because small quality problems may become visible when the image is enlarged. It is also important to avoid repeatedly compressing the same JPG. Each lossy re-encoding can add further quality loss. Keep the original camera or editing file and create a separate compressed copy.

sections.heading: Does JPG Compression Change Image Dimensions?
sections.body: No. The image tools preserve original display dimensions and do not provide a resize option. EXIF orientation may be normalized so an upright photograph has different stored width and height while keeping its displayed orientation.

sections.heading: Is the JPG Compressor Private?
sections.body: Selected images are processed in your browser rather than uploaded to a compression server. Each image can be up to 50 MiB and 32 megapixels. Queues allow up to 500 files and 300 MiB in total. Browser memory can still limit processing below these bounds. Keep a source copy before trying a new encoding.

faq.q: Can I compress JPG images without changing their dimensions?
faq.a: Yes. Original display dimensions are preserved. Image resizing is not offered.

faq.q: Can I reduce a JPG to 100KB or 50KB?
faq.a: You can use Target Size to attempt a maximum file size. Whether the target is achievable depends on the photograph and acceptable quality.

faq.q: Is JPG the same as JPEG?
faq.a: Yes. JPG and JPEG refer to the same image format. The difference is mainly in the file extension.

faq.q: Why is my compressed JPG not smaller?
faq.a: The original photograph may already be efficiently compressed. If no smaller suitable result is found, the original is retained unchanged.
